Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 1:

﴿Take not My enemy and your enemy as friends﴾. The word ʿaduww (enemy) applies to one person and to a group, and what is meant here is the disbelievers of Quraysh. This verse was revealed concerning Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Balta‘ah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to go out to Makkah in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, but he gave a misleading indication of that by mentioning Khaybar. So it spread among the people that he was going out to Khaybar, while he himself informed a group of his senior companions of his intention to go to Makkah. Among them was Ḥāṭib, who then wrote to some people of Makkah informing them of this. News of it came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from heaven. So he sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Zubayr and al-Miqdād, and said: "Set off until you reach Rawdat Khākh, for there is a woman traveller with her a letter from Ḥāṭib to the polytheists." They set off until they found the woman, and said to her: "Bring out the letter." She said: "I have no letter with me." They searched all of her baggage but found nothing, and some of them said: "She has no letter with her." ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has not lied, nor has Allah lied. By Allah, you will either bring out the letter or we will strip you." She said: "Turn away from me," so she brought it out from the braids and hair-locks of her head. It was also said: she brought it out from her waistband. They brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to Ḥāṭib: "Who wrote this?" He said: "I did, O Messenger of Allah. But do not be hasty with me. By Allah, I did not do this as an apostasy from my religion, nor out of desire for disbelief. Rather, I was a man attached to Quraysh without being one of them by lineage, and I wanted to have a favour with them by which they would look after my relatives." ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, to strike the neck of this hypocrite." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ḥāṭib has spoken the truth. He is among the people of Badr. And what could make you know, O ʿUmar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do what you will, for I have forgiven you.'" And: "Say nothing to Ḥāṭib except good." So the verse was revealed as a rebuke to Ḥāṭib and a warning against anyone doing the like of his deed; yet within it, along with that, is an honouring of him, because Allah bore witness to his faith in His saying "O you who have believed."

﴿You convey to them affection﴾. This is an expression for conveying affection to them. The verb alqā (to cast/convey) takes a preposition and also takes none, as in His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 39]. This sentence is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿Take not﴾, or in the position of a qualifier of awliyā', or a new sentence (istiʾnāf). ﴿And they have disbelieved﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿Take not﴾ or in tulqūn. ﴿They expel the Messenger and you﴾, i.e., they expel the Messenger and expel you: meaning their expelling of them from Makkah, for they constricted them and harmed them until they went out from it as emigrants to Madinah, and some of them went out to the land of Abyssinia. ﴿Because you believe﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), i.e., they expel you on account of your faith. ﴿If you have gone out in struggle in My way﴾: the response of this conditional is omitted, being indicated by what precedes it, and it is: "do not take." The meaning is: if you have gone out in struggle in My way and seeking My pleasure, then do not take My enemy and your enemy as friends. Jihādan (in struggle) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause or an object of purpose, and likewise ibtighāʾ (seeking).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 2:

﴿If they overcome you﴾ means: if they gain the upper hand over you. ﴿And they would love that you disbelieve﴾ means: they wish that you would disbelieve, so that you would be like them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'wadda' (they loved) in the past tense after mentioning the response of the condition in the present tense, because they wanted your disbelief before anything else."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 3:

﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; He will separate between you.﴾ This is a reference to what Hatib intended by protecting his kinship. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you.﴾ It may be from separation in the sense of judging between them, or from separation in the sense of dividing, meaning that He will divide you from your relatives on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said that the governing element (al-'amil) of "on the Day of Resurrection" is what precedes it, but that is far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 4:

﴿Indeed there was for you a good example in Abraham and those with him﴾. The uswa (ʾuswah, example) is that which one follows. So Allah commanded the Muslims to follow Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, and those who were with him in enmity toward the disbelievers and in disassociating from them. And the meaning of "those with him" is those among the people who believed in him. It has also been said that it refers to the prophets who were in his time and close to his time. Ibn ʿAtiyyah preferred this view on the basis of what is reported in the hadith: that Abraham, peace be upon him, said to his wife, "There is no believer on the earth other than me and you."

﴿Innocent (bura'a')﴾, the plural of barii' (innocent, free). ﴿We disbelieve in you﴾, meaning: we deny you in your statements. It may also be an expression for extreme hatred and severance from them. ﴿Except the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾. This is an exception from the phrase "a good example." The meaning is: follow them in their enmity toward the disbelievers, but do not follow them in this, because Abraham promised his father that he would seek forgiveness for him; then, when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. It has also been said that the exception applies to the disassociation and severance, and the meaning is: Abraham and those with him disassociated from the disbelievers, except that Abraham had promised his father to seek forgiveness for him. ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾. This is from the speech of our master Abraham, peace be upon him, and those with him, and it is connected to what came before the exception, so it is among what they were commanded to follow.

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. In its meaning there are two opinions. The first: Do not grant them victory over us, for that would become a trial for them and a cause of their misguidance; for they would say, "We have overcome them," and that would be for them, because we are upon the truth and they are upon falsehood. The second: Do not give them power over us, so that they tempt us away from our religion. Ibn 'Atiyya (Ibn 'Atiyyah) preferred this, because it is a supplication for themselves; whereas according to the first opinion it is a supplication for the disbelievers. But the intent is not a supplication for the disbelievers; rather it is a supplication for themselves for victory, in such a way that the disbelievers are not tempted by it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 7:

﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity.﴾ When Allah commanded the Muslims to be hostile to the disbelievers and to cut off relations with them, they complied, even though there were ties of kinship between them and the disbelievers. Allah knew their sincerity, so He comforted them with this verse and promised them that He would place affection between them. This affection was fulfilled at the conquest of Makkah, for at that time all of the Quraysh embraced Islam. It has also been said that the affection was the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Habibah bint Abi Sufyan ibn Harb, the chief of the Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyyah rejected this view on the ground that the marriage of Umm Habibah took place before the revelation of this verse.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 60, verse 8:

﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾ Allah granted the Muslims permission to show kindness to those disbelievers who did not fight them. Scholars differed about who these people were, giving four opinions. The first is that they were tribes of the Arabs, among them Khuza'ah and Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, who had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would not fight him and would not help anyone against him. The second is that they were some of the disbelievers of Quraysh who did not fight the Muslims and did not drive them out of Makkah; according to these two opinions, the verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by the command to fight. The third is that they were women and children; on this view it is reported that Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has come to me while she is a polytheist; should I maintain ties with her?" He said: "Yes, maintain ties with your mother." The fourth is that the verse means those believers in Makkah who had not emigrated, whereas those whose friendship Allah forbade, because they fought the Muslims and backed the expulsion of them, are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 10:

﴿O you who have believed, when the believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them.﴾ Meaning: examine them, so that you may know the sincerity of their faith. He called them "believing women" only because of their outward condition. Scholars have differed about this testing, into three opinions. The first is that the woman is made to swear that she did not emigrate out of hatred for her husband, nor out of fear, nor for any other worldly aim apart from the love of Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode. The second is that the shahada, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, is presented to her. The third is that the conditions mentioned after this are presented to her: abandoning association with Allah, theft, killing their children, abandoning adultery, slander, and disobedience. If she acknowledges these, that is her test. This was related from Ayesha, may Allah be pleased with her. ﴿So if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers.﴾ This verse was revealed after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, and that treaty had included that the Muslims would return to the disbelievers everyone who came to them as a Muslim, men and women. Allah abrogated (naskh) the ruling concerning the women by this verse, and forbade returning a believing woman to the disbelievers when she emigrates to the Muslims. The woman who emigrated at that time was Umaymah bint Bishr, the wife of Hassan ibn al-Dahdahah. It is also said it was Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah. When she emigrated, her husband came and said, "O Muhammad, return her to us, for that is within the condition you have with us." So the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) tested her and did not return her, and he gave her husband her dowry (mahr). It is also said that it was revealed concerning Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who fled from her husband to the Muslims. Scholars differed over whether the ruling on men is the same as on women, so that a truce may not permit returning any Muslim man, or whether it is still permissible, on two opinions. The more apparent view is that it is permissible, because what was abrogated was only the ruling concerning the women. ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them.﴾ This is the justification for forbidding the return of the woman to the disbelievers, and it contains evidence that the marriage between polytheists and Muslim women has ended.

﴿And give them what they have spent.﴾ That is, give the disbelievers what they had spent on their wives as dowries when those women emigrated. Then He permitted the Muslims to marry them upon payment of the dowry. ﴿And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women.﴾ Al-'Isam is the plural of 'ismah, meaning the marriage bond. So Allah commanded the Muslims to separate from their disbelieving wives, meaning the female polytheists who worship idols. On this view the verse is muhkam (definitive). It is also said that it means every disbelieving woman. On this view, from it the permissibility of marrying women of the People of the Book was abrogated, by His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning a wife of Umar ibn al-Khattab who was a disbeliever, and he divorced her. ﴿And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent.﴾ That is, demand from the disbelievers what you spent as dowries on your wives who fled to the disbelievers, and let the disbelievers demand from you what they spent on their wives who emigrated to the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 11:

﴿And if any of your wives have gone over to the disbelievers, and you then have a turn of victory, give to those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent.﴾

The meaning of "if any of your wives have gone over to the disbelievers" is: the fleeing of the wives of the Muslims to the disbelievers. The address in His words "and you then have a turn of victory, give to those whose wives have gone" is to the Muslims. His words "you have a turn of victory" (ʿaqabtum) are not from punishment for a sin; rather, it is from ʿuqba (the outcome), meaning you obtained an outcome, which is booty (ghanima). Or it is from al-taʿaqub (alternation) over a thing, as two men take turns riding an animal, this one once and that one another time. Since some of the wives of the Muslims fled to the disbelievers and some of the wives of the disbelievers fled to the Muslims, this was treated as an alternation over the women.

The occasion of revelation of the verse was that when God said: ﴿And ask for back what you have spent, and let them ask for back what they have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahina: 10], the disbelievers said: "We do not accept this ruling, and we will not give the dowry of whoever's wife has fled to us from the Muslims." So God revealed this other verse and commanded the Muslims to pay the dowry to those whose wives had fled to the Muslims from the disbelievers. This paid amount is to come from the spoils of war (maghanim), according to the view of one who said that the meaning of "you have a turn of victory" is "you gained booty." It was also said: it is from the fay' (property taken without battle). It was also said: it is from the charities that were given to the disbelievers when their wives fled to the Muslims, and God revealed that they be given to them when they did not accept His ruling.

The rulings contained in this verse have been abrogated, because it was revealed concerning specific cases, namely the truce of the Prophet ﷺ with the polytheists of the Arabs. Then these rulings ended with the ending of the truce, so it is not permissible to make a truce with the polytheists of the Arabs; for them there is only Islam or the sword. A truce is permissible only with the People of the Book and the Magians, because God said concerning the polytheists: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], and said concerning the People of the Book: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾ [al-Tawba: 29], and the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the Magians: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book."

ۧ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾. This pledge is the pledge of the women on the second day of the Conquest (of Makkah), at Mount al-Safa. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would take their pledge by speech, and his hand would not touch the hand of any woman. This is related in the authentic hadith from ʿĀʾishah.

﴿And that they will not bring a slander (buhtan) forged by themselves﴾. Its meaning according to the majority (al-jumhur) is that a woman attributes to her husband a child that is not his. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah chose that buhtan here be general, so that a woman attributes to a man someone other than his child, or slanders anyone with speech, or lies about what Allah has entrusted to her, such as menstruation and pregnancy, and other things.

﴿And that they will not disobey you in what is right (maʿruf)﴾, i.e., they will not disobey you in what the Sharia has brought of commands and prohibitions. Among that is the prohibition of wailing (niyahah), tearing the collars (shaqq al-juyub), attaching hair extensions (wasl al-shaʿr), and other things that the women of the Jahiliyyah used to do. It is related in a hadith that when the women pledged this pledge to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he required them not to steal. Hind bint ʿUtbah, who was the wife of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abu Sufyan is a stingy man. Is it upon me if I take from his wealth without his permission?" He said to her: "Take what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner (bil-maʿruf)."

When he required them not to commit fornication, Hind said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a free woman commit fornication?" The Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be peace, said: "A free woman does not commit fornication," meaning in the generality of women, because fornication among the Quraysh was only practiced by slave women. When he said, "and that they will not kill their children," she said: "We raised them when they were small, and you killed them when they were grown at Badr," so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed. When he made them stand firm on not disobeying him in what is right, she said: "We did not sit in this gathering while we had in our hearts that we would disobey you."

This pledge for women is not practiced today, because the scholars have unanimously agreed that the imam is not entitled to stipulate these conditions upon them. Either it is abrogated (mansukhah) and the abrogating text was not mentioned, or the leaving of these conditions is because they have been established and known from the Sharia by necessity, so there is no need to stipulate them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 60, verse 13:

﴿Do not take as allies a people with whom God is angry﴾ He means the Jews. Some of the poor among the Muslims used to show affection toward them in order to obtain some of their wealth. It is also said that he means the disbelievers of Quraysh. The first view is more apparent, because anger has become a established description of the Jews, as in His words: ﴿not of those who have earned anger⁠—﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] ﴿They have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾. For one who says that the people with whom God is angry are the Jews, the meaning of "they have despaired of the Hereafter" is that they have despaired of the good of the Hereafter and of happiness in it. For one who says that the people with whom God is angry are the disbelievers of Quraysh, the meaning is that they have despaired of the existence of the Hereafter and of its reality, since they flatly deny it. As for His words ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾, it admits of two interpretations. The first is that it means: just as the disbelievers who deny resurrection have despaired of the resurrection of those in the graves; thus the phrase ﴿of those in the graves﴾ is connected to "despaired" and the text omits a word (an elided genitive, muḍāf). The second is that ﴿of those in the graves﴾ is explanatory of the category, meaning: just as those who are in the graves have despaired of happiness in the Hereafter, because they are certain that they will be punished therein.
